lead: After this unit you can name every part of a data communication system, place any network on the LAN–MAN–WAN ladder, and draw both the OSI and the TCP/IP stacks from memory. You can also compare circuit and packet switching with numbers, and say exactly what a hub, a switch and a router each do to a frame.
about: This unit builds the vocabulary the rest of the subject uses. Chapter 1.1 defines data communication, its five components and the three flow modes. Chapter 1.2 groups networks by span into LAN, MAN and WAN. Chapter 1.3 shows how nodes are wired, with the cost formulas for mesh and star. Chapter 1.4 introduces protocols, standards and layering, and names the protocol data units. Chapter 1.5 lays out the seven OSI layers; Chapter 1.6 compresses them into the TCP/IP suite and shows how the Internet is built from edges, access links and an ISP core. Chapter 1.7 contrasts circuit and packet switching, the two ways of moving bits across those layers. Chapter 1.8 ends with the hardware that does it: hubs, bridges, switches and routers.

chapters.idea: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through five parts — message, sender, receiver, medium and protocol — and the data can flow in one direction, both directions in turn, or both directions at once.
chapters.depth: Define data communication and list the five components with one example each. Give one line per form of data representation: text, numbers, images, audio, video. Cover the three direction-of-flow modes — simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex — with the standard examples and the utilisation and turnaround-time penalty of half-duplex; some syllabi call these transmission modes. Cover types of connection: point-to-point and multipoint (multi-drop). Close with the three network criteria: performance, reliability, security. Keep the arithmetic of bandwidth and capacity for the next unit.

figure.title: Five components of data communication
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain of source, transmitter, transmission medium, receiver and destination, with the medium highlighted as the shared part between the two ends.

chapters.example: A customer books a ticket on IRCTC and the app shows a PNR. (a) Name the five components for this transfer. (b) State the flow mode in each of these cases: the server pushes a bank statement to your app and you can only read it; a teller terminal sends one request and waits for the reply before sending the next; two engineers talk on a video call. Answer: (a) message = the booking request and the PNR screen; sender = phone; receiver = IRCTC server; medium = the mobile data or Wi-Fi link plus the provider's network; protocol = HTTPS over TCP/IP. (b) statement push = simplex; request-reply = half-duplex; video call = full-duplex.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the sender with the transmitter and the receiver with the destination: the computer is the sender or receiver, the modem or NIC is the transmitter or receiver. A second trap is calling a normal telephone call half-duplex.
chapters.leave: Signal shapes, bandwidth, attenuation and noise belong to Unit 2; error checking and framing belong to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Networks are classified by span and by who owns them: a LAN covers a room to a campus and is owned by one organisation, a MAN covers a city and is run by a provider, and a WAN crosses states or countries on provider links.
chapters.depth: Give PAN (a few metres, Bluetooth), LAN (one building or campus, one owner, high speed, shared or switched medium), MAN (one city, metro Ethernet, cable TV and ISP backbones), WAN (leased lines and switched WAN, provider owned, long distance), and internetwork (two or more networks joined; the Internet is the largest). Add one line on access networks versus the core. Contrast LAN and WAN on ownership, speed, error rate and cost per bit. Also contrast a private WAN link with a VPN over the Internet.

figure.title: Network categories by span
figure.aria: A four-step ladder from LAN to MAN to WAN to internetwork, showing increasing span, with the LAN highlighted as the one network a single organisation owns.

chapters.example: A firm has three offices inside Chennai joined by a provider's metro Ethernet service, and one office in Dubai joined by a 34 Mbps WAN link. (a) Name each network type. (b) How long does a 68 MB file take to reach Dubai, ignoring overhead? Answer: (a) the three Chennai offices plus the metro service form a MAN; the Dubai link is a WAN; together they are an internetwork. (b) 68 MB = 68 × 8 = 544 Mbit = 544 × 10⁶ bits. Time = 544 × 10⁶ ÷ 34 × 10⁶ = 16 s.
chapters.trap: Judging LAN, MAN and WAN by distance alone. A 40 km link inside one company is still a private WAN-style link, and Wi-Fi inside one building is still a LAN. Ownership and technology separate them as much as span.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1, for the five components that make up any single network.
chapters.leave: Physical media used by each network type are in Unit 2; switching inside the WAN is in Chapter 1.7.

chapters.idea: A topology is the pattern in which links join nodes, and each pattern trades cable and port cost against fault tolerance and easy growth.
chapters.depth: Cover mesh (full and partial), star, bus, ring, tree and hybrid. For each: how a frame travels, number of links and ports, cost, behaviour when one link or node fails, and ease of adding a node. Give the mesh formulas: links = n(n − 1)/2, ports per node = n − 1; and the star facts: n cables, one central device with n ports, single point of failure at the centre. Mention logical versus physical topology in one line, and that a star-bus or star-ring is what real campuses use.

figure.aria: A star topology with four PCs each joined by one link to a single central switch, so every frame passes through the centre.

chapters.example: A lab has 8 computers. Compare a full mesh and a star. Mesh: links = 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 cables, and each computer needs 7 ports. Star: 8 cables to one switch, 8 switch ports, 1 port per computer. With each cable run 20 m at ₹30 per metre, the star needs 8 × 20 = 160 m, costing ₹4,800; the mesh needs at least 28 × 20 = 560 m, costing ₹16,800. The mesh survives any single cable cut; the star dies completely if the switch fails.
chapters.trap: Writing n(n − 1) links for a mesh and forgetting the ÷ 2, because one cable serves both ends. Then the cost comes out exactly double.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2, to know which topology suits a LAN, a MAN and a WAN.
chapters.leave: Access methods on a shared bus or ring, such as CSMA/CD, are in Unit 3; the switch itself is in Chapter 1.8.

chapters.idea: A protocol is an agreed set of rules with syntax, semantics and timing, and layering splits one big problem into layers that each serve the layer above and talk to their own peer through headers.
chapters.depth: Define protocol and its three elements with examples. Explain layering: service, interface, peer process; each layer adds a header (encapsulation) and the receiver strips it. Name the PDUs: message, segment, packet, frame, bits. Cover standards: de facto versus de jure, and the bodies ISO, ITU-T, IEEE and IETF with RFCs. Give the benefits of layering (modularity, vendor independence, easier teaching) and the costs (header overhead, some duplicated function, a layer cannot easily use a lower layer's detail).

figure.aria: A five-step stack in which application data becomes a segment, then a packet, then a frame, then bits on the medium, with the packet stage highlighted.

chapters.example: A 1,500-byte application message is sent over Ethernet. Headers are TCP 20 bytes, IP 20 bytes, Ethernet 14 bytes, plus a 4-byte frame check trailer. (a) Find the frame size and the efficiency. (b) Repeat for a 10-byte message. Answer: (a) 1500 + 20 + 20 + 14 + 4 = 1,558 bytes; overhead 58 bytes; efficiency = 1500 ÷ 1558 = 96.3%. (b) 10 + 58 = 68 bytes; efficiency = 10 ÷ 68 = 14.7%. Small messages are dominated by headers.
chapters.trap: Saying layer N on one host talks to layer N + 1 on the other host. Peers are always at the same layer; the data moves down and up only inside each host.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3, since layering assumes links and nodes already exist.
chapters.leave: The actual header fields and bit-level encoding are in Units 3, 4 and 5; standards bodies are only named here.

chapters.idea: The OSI model is a seven-layer reference model that gives each networking job exactly one home, from bits on the wire up to the user's application.
chapters.depth: Go bottom-up through physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. For each layer give the job, its PDU, one or two protocols and the devices that work there. Give the interfaces between adjacent layers and the idea of a reference model that is not itself a protocol suite. Say plainly that OSI is a teaching and design model and that the Internet uses TCP/IP; give the standard criticism that session and presentation are thin in real software. Include a small mapping of OSI layers to TCP/IP layers, but keep the full suite for the next chapter.

figure.aria: The seven OSI layers stacked from application at the top to physical at the bottom, with the transport and network layers highlighted as the two the exams test most.

chapters.example: Name the OSI layer for each task. (a) Encrypting a file before sending. (b) Choosing a route across three routers. (c) Retransmitting a lost segment. (d) Turning bits into an electrical signal. (e) Keeping a user logged in across many requests. (f) Adding port numbers. (g) Adding a MAC address and a check trailer. Answers: (a) presentation, (b) network, (c) transport, (d) physical, (e) session, (f) transport, (g) data link.
chapters.trap: Placing encryption in the transport layer, routing in the data link layer, or calling OSI a protocol suite. OSI is a model; it defines no headers of its own.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4, for protocols, encapsulation and PDU names.
chapters.leave: Layer-by-layer protocol detail is in Units 3 to 6; the address formats are in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The Internet runs on the TCP/IP suite, a four-layer stack whose narrow waist is IP, and its architecture is an edge of hosts and access links joined to a core of routers run by ISPs.
chapters.depth: Give the four layers — network access (link plus physical), internet, transport, application — and the five-layer teaching version with a separate physical layer, since many Indian textbooks use five. List protocols per layer: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP, DHCP at the top; TCP, UDP; IP, ICMP, ARP; Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP. State IP's contract: connectionless, best-effort, unreliable, with no order guarantee. Describe the architecture: edge (hosts, access networks), core (routers, ISP tiers, exchange points), and the path a packet takes. Give the OSI-to-TCP/IP mapping and one line on the end-to-end argument.

figure.aria: The four TCP/IP layers from application down to network access, with the transport layer highlighted as the one that adds reliability on top of a best-effort IP.

chapters.example: Place each protocol in its TCP/IP layer and say whether it is end-to-end or hop-by-hop: HTTP, DNS, TCP, UDP, IP, ICMP, ARP, Ethernet, Wi-Fi, SMTP. Answer: application — HTTP, DNS, SMTP; transport — TCP, UDP (end-to-end); internet — IP and ICMP (end-to-end), and ARP, which sits on the boundary between the internet and network access layers because it carries IP addresses inside link frames; network access — Ethernet, Wi-Fi (hop-by-hop).
chapters.trap: Drawing seven TCP/IP layers by copying OSI, or claiming the network access layer is only the data link layer. In the four-layer model it also covers the physical layer.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.5, so the OSI names can be mapped rather than relearned.
chapters.leave: TCP and UDP behaviour is Unit 5; real applications, DNS and HTTP are Unit 6; addressing and routing are Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Circuit switching reserves a fixed path for the whole call, while packet switching chops data into packets that share links store-and-forward, so it wastes less capacity but gives variable delay.
chapters.depth: Circuit switching: the three phases of setup, data transfer and teardown; a dedicated path; multiplexing inside the link by FDM or TDM; constant rate, fixed delay, guaranteed bandwidth; capacity wasted when the caller is silent. Packet switching: store-and-forward at each router, statistical multiplexing, header overhead, queuing delay and jitter, possible reordering. Distinguish datagram (each packet routed alone) from virtual circuit (a fixed path, no bandwidth reserved). Compare on setup delay, delay variation, efficiency for bursty traffic, per-packet overhead, and billing. Keep the delay formulas simple and state assumptions.

figure.aria: Two timelines: the circuit line pays a setup phase before any data moves and a teardown after, while the packet line starts sending packets at once and pays only per-packet store-and-forward.

chapters.example: A 1 MB file crosses three links of 1 Mbps each; ignore headers, queuing and propagation. (a) Circuit switching with 0.5 s setup and 0.5 s teardown. (b) Packet switching with 1,000-byte packets. Answer: 1 MB = 8 × 10⁶ bits = 8 Mbit; sending once over one link takes 8 × 10⁶ ÷ 10⁶ = 8 s. (a) 0.5 + 8 + 0.5 = 9 s. (b) 1,000 packets of 8,000 bits each take 8 ms per link; the last packet finishes after 8 s + 2 × 8 ms = 8.016 s. Packet switching wins here because setup dominates for short transfers.
chapters.trap: Charging setup time to every packet, or forgetting that each hop stores the whole packet before forwarding, so delay grows with the number of hops.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.6, to know which layer holds packets and which holds the call.
chapters.leave: The switching fabric design and multiplexing hierarchies are in Unit 2; link-layer access on a shared medium is in Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Each device works at one layer: a hub repeats bits into one collision domain, a bridge or switch forwards frames by MAC address, and a router forwards packets by IP address between networks.
chapters.depth: Treat repeater and hub (layer 1, shared bandwidth, half duplex, one collision domain), bridge and switch (layer 2, learn source MAC, forward known destinations, flood unknown and broadcast frames, one collision domain per port, full duplex, still one broadcast domain; VLANs can split it and are named only), router (layer 3, IP lookup, new MAC header per hop, separates broadcast domains), plus one line each on NIC, access point and gateway. Cover the three switch actions: learn, forward, flood. Define collision domain and broadcast domain and count them for a small figure.

figure.aria: A hierarchy with a router at the top joining two switches; the hub under Switch 1 puts PC 1, PC 2 and PC 3 in one collision domain, while PC 4 has its own.

chapters.example: A switch with ports 1 to 4 starts with an empty MAC table. Frames arrive: (1) A to B on port 1; (2) B to A on port 2; (3) A to C on port 1; (4) C to A on port 3. Fill the table and say where each frame goes. Answer: (1) learn A on 1, destination B unknown, flood to 2, 3, 4. (2) learn B on 2; A is known on 1, forward to port 1 only. (3) A already on 1; C unknown, flood to 2, 3, 4, never back out of port 1. (4) learn C on 3; forward to port 1. Final table: A on 1, B on 2, C on 3.
chapters.trap: Saying a switch separates broadcast domains. It separates collision domains only; a broadcast frame still floods every port until a router or a VLAN boundary stops it.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.5 and 1.6, to attach each device to its layer, and Chapter 1.7, for what a switch actually switches.
chapters.leave: MAC addresses and Ethernet frames are in Unit 3; IP lookup tables and routing protocols are in Unit 4; VLAN detail is in Unit 3.

links: One network has five components; many such networks form a LAN, MAN or WAN
Once the network type is fixed, the nodes must be wired in a topology
A topology is only links and nodes; protocols make them exchange data
The layering idea becomes the seven-layer OSI model
The OSI model is mapped onto the four-layer TCP/IP suite that the Internet uses
Layered packets travel through the network by circuit or packet switching
Switching is done by real devices: hubs, bridges, switches and routers
